summary: Describes how SNMPv1, SNMPv2, and SNMPv3 can coexist, and how to convert between the information definitions of the older frameworks and the newer ones. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3584 explains how SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 systems can coexist. It defines translation rules for MIBs, notifications and requests, and explains how older community strings map into SNMPv3 access controls.

questions: how do snmpv1 and snmpv3 work together
how to convert smiv1 mib to smiv2

how does an snmp proxy translate traps
subtitle: How SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 exchange management data and translate between formats.

tldr.problem: Networks may contain devices using three SNMP framework versions, with differences in MIB descriptions, notifications, operations and errors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3584 specifies SMIv1-to-SMIv2 conversion, notification and error mappings, multilingual agents and proxies, and a MIB that maps community strings into SNMPv3 parameters.
tldr.outcome: The coexistence procedures help older and newer systems communicate, but translation to SNMPv1 loses authentication and privacy. RFC 3584 obsoletes RFC 2576.

today: RFC 3584 is Best Current Practice (BCP 74), published in August 2003. It obsoletes RFC 2576 and recommends deploying SNMPv3 with cryptographic security.

sections.title: Three SNMP Framework Versions
sections.content:
RFC 3584 covers coexistence among SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3. It addresses conversion of MIB documents between SMIv1 and SMIv2, translation of notification parameters, communication between multilingual systems and proxies, and integration of community-based versions with the SNMP architecture.

SNMPv3 uses SNMPv2 protocol operations and MIB definitions. In this RFC, many rules about SNMPv2 operations therefore also apply to SNMPv3.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP has three framework versions with different message and data formats. This RFC describes how an agent or proxy can translate between them.

sections.title: Converting SMIv1 MIB Modules
sections.content:
To make an SMIv1 MIB module conform to SMIv2, its imports, macros, access clauses, status values and object groups must be updated. For example, Counter becomes Counter32, Gauge becomes Gauge32 or Unsigned32, and ACCESS becomes MAX-ACCESS. Trap definitions become notification definitions with the corresponding object identifiers.

Conversion does not by itself require deprecating objects. The RFC also describes how to preserve compatibility when an index uses NetworkAddress and lists other recommended improvements, such as defining units and bounds.
sections.plainLanguage: An older MIB description needs its fields and declarations updated to match SMIv2. The managed objects can keep their meaning even when their descriptions change.

sections.title: Translating Notification Parameters
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 use different fields to describe notifications. Translating from v1 to v2 copies the timestamp to sysUpTime and maps the generic and specific trap values to an snmpTrapOID. Translating in the other direction maps the OID back to v1 trap fields.

A proxy may add bindings to preserve the original agent address, community string and enterprise. A notification containing a Counter64 value cannot be encoded for SNMPv1, so it cannot be sent or forwarded using that version.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator maps the fields that one version can express into the other version's format. If an SNMPv2 notification contains Counter64, SNMPv1 cannot carry it.

sections.title: Multilingual Agents and Managers
sections.content:
A multilingual implementation supports several message versions and selects one for each peer. When it sends a GetBulk request using SNMPv1, it changes it to GetNext because SNMPv1 has no GetBulk operation.

When an SNMPv1 request reaches an agent that uses SNMPv2 data access, Counter64 objects are treated as outside the available view. The responder does not return a Counter64 value in an SNMPv1 response. It also maps SNMPv2 exceptions and error statuses into the smaller set of SNMPv1 results.
sections.plainLanguage: A multilingual agent speaks the version selected for each peer. If that version cannot represent a value or operation, the agent skips it or returns the closest supported error.

sections.title: Proxies Between Versions
sections.content:
A proxy lets two systems that support different SNMP versions communicate by translating their protocol data units. The RFC defines different rules depending on which version is used on the upstream and downstream sides.

For example, a GetBulk sent downstream using SNMPv1 becomes GetNext. When a newer response contains Counter64 or exceptions that SNMPv1 cannot represent, the proxy may return noSuchName or repeat GetNext while skipping Counter64 objects. Inform requests cannot be forwarded over SNMPv1.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy translates requests and responses between the two versions. Some operations need to be simplified, and some newer values cannot pass through an SNMPv1 connection.

sections.title: Community Strings and the Community MIB
sections.content:
SNMP-COMMUNITY-MIB maps a community string to a security name, context engine ID and context name, and can map those parameters back to a community string. This lets community-based SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c requests use view-based access control in the SNMP architecture.

The MIB can also validate a request's source address and select community strings for outgoing notifications. A transport-address mask can let a target entry match a range of addresses rather than only one address.
sections.plainLanguage: The Community MIB connects an older community string to SNMPv3's names and contexts. Access-control views can then limit which management objects the request may reach.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 do not provide security themselves. Mapping a community name to a security name and context allows view-based access controls to limit access, but a proxy that forwards an authenticated and private SNMPv3 message over SNMPv1 loses those protections.

The community table can create or expose community strings, so access to it should be restricted. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic authentication and privacy and does not recommend deploying earlier versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Translation through SNMPv1 removes SNMPv3 authentication and privacy. Restrict community-table access and use SNMPv3 with cryptographic security where possible.
